claims.claim: IFN-α pretreatment results in a much more dramatic repression of viral replication in USP18-KD (~15 times more effective than in WT).
claims.source: We found that the IFN-α pretreatment resulted in a much more dramatic repression of viral replication in USP18-KD, ~15 times more effective than in WT (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), indicating that USP18-mediated desensitization attenuates the antiviral effect of prolonged IFN-α pretreatment.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from viral replication assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: USP18-mediated desensitization attenuates the antiviral effect of prolonged IFN-α pretreatment.
claims.source: We found that the IFN-α pretreatment resulted in a much more dramatic repression of viral replication in USP18-KD, ~15 times more effective than in WT (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), indicating that USP18-mediated desensitization attenuates the antiviral effect of prolonged IFN-α pretreatment.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of viral replication between WT and USP18-KD cells with IFN-α pretreatment.

claims.claim: The computational model suggests that a prolonged input is required to initiate USP18 upregulation.
claims.source: In summary, our modeling results suggest that a prolonged input is required to initiate USP18 upregulation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results showing that a delay in USP18 upregulation is necessary to reproduce experimental observations.

claims.claim: The fitting error between model simulations and experimental data reaches the minimum when the delay time in USP18 upregulation is 8 hours.
claims.source: By fitting the model to the data for each assigned delay time, we found that the fitting error (between simulations and data) reaches the minimum when the delay time is 8 hrs (Figure 3, B and C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1, B–E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling and fitting to experimental data, as shown in Figure 3, B and C.

claims.claim: Repetitive transient IFN inputs shorter than the delay time lead to a higher transcriptional response than a prolonged input with the same total treatment time.
claims.source: The model further predicted that repetitive transient IFN inputs that are shorter than the delay time could be less able to induce the USP18-mediated negative feedback loop and hence could lead to a higher transcriptional response than that induced by a prolonged input with the same total treatment time.
claims.evidence: This claim is a prediction from the computational model.

claims.claim: Pulsatile IFN inputs with 5 × 8-hr pulses produce a higher transcriptional response than a 40-hr sustained input.
claims.source: This prediction was tested experimentally and a higher transcriptional response, indicated by the PIRF9-driven reporter, was observed when 5 × 8-hr IFN pulses were given, compared to that induced by a single 40-hr treatment.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing pulsatile versus sustained IFN inputs.

claims.claim: The difference in transcriptional response between pulsatile and sustained IFN inputs is abolished in USP18-KD cells.
claims.source: Furthermore, this difference caused by different input dynamics was abolished in USP18-KD cells (Figure 3F; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: IRF9 and USP18, although induced by the same upstream JAK-STAT signaling, exhibit strikingly different activation times.
claims.source: We found that, consistent with our model, IRF9 and USP18, although induced by the same upstream JAK-STAT signaling, exhibited strikingly different activation times.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the dual reporter cell line tracking IRF9 and USP18 expression.

claims.claim: PIRF9-driven expression is induced with a fast and relatively uniform kinetics among cells.
claims.source: PIRF9-driven expression was induced with a fast and relatively uniform kinetics among cells; in contrast, PUSP18-driven expression exhibited a slow and heterogeneous kinetics (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: PUSP18-driven expression exhibits a slow and heterogeneous kinetics.
claims.source: PIRF9-driven expression was induced with a fast and relatively uniform kinetics among cells; in contrast, PUSP18-driven expression exhibited a slow and heterogeneous kinetics (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: About 83.3% of cells show modest delays in USP18 induction (<10 hrs), whereas 16.7% of cells exhibit more prolonged delays (>10 hrs).
claims.source: Intriguingly, we quantified the delay times of UPS18 induction, relative to that of IRF9, in single cells and observed a long-tail distribution: about 83.3% of cells showed modest delays in induction (<10 hrs), whereas the other 16.7% cells exhibited more prolonged delays (>10 hrs).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data quantifying delay times in single cells.

claims.claim: The mean activation times of IRF9 and USP18 are 7.9008 ± 0.1914 and 12.1620 ± 0.2349 hrs, respectively.
claims.source: The mean activation times (with 95% confidence interval) of IRF9 and USP18 are 7.9008 ± 0.1914 and 12.1620 ± 0.2349 hrs, respectively.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Cells show modest delays in USP18 induction if IFN treatment is added at the early phase of their cell cycles (0–35% of the cell cycle).
claims.source: We found that cells showed modest delays if the treatment was added at the early phase of their cell cycles (0–35% of the cell cycle).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data analyzing the relationship between cell cycle stage and USP18 delay time.

claims.claim: In cells that progressed beyond the early phase of cell cycle, IFN treatment cannot initiate USP18 induction until the next cell cycle, resulting in extended delay times.
claims.source: In contrast, in those cells that progressed beyond this phase, the IFN treatment could not initiate USP18 induction until the next cell cycle, resulting in extended delay times proportional to the times needed to reach the next cell cycle (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: Cell-to-cell variability in USP18 delay times stems from different cell cycle stages among cells at the treatment onset.
claims.source: These results suggest that the cell-to-cell variability in USP18 delay times may stem from different cell cycle stages among cells at the treatment onset.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing the relationship between cell cycle stage and USP18 delay time.

claims.claim: Cell cycle synchronization substantially reduces the fraction of cells with prolonged delays of USP18 induction.
claims.source: As expected, we observed that cell cycle synchronization substantially reduced the fraction of cells with prolonged delays of USP18 induction (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using cell cycle synchronization methods shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: G1 and S cells show relatively fast USP18 activation times, whereas a large fraction of G2 cells exhibit a substantial delay in USP18 induction.
claims.source: We found that G1 and S cells showed relatively fast USP18 activation times, whereas a large fraction of G2 cells exhibited a substantial delay in USP18 induction (Figure 5C, right).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using the CDK2 activity reporter shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The G1/S stages allow rapid induction of USP18 expression, but the G2 stage restrains the initiation of gene induction, resulting in a prolonged delay in USP18 expression.
claims.source: These results, together with the cell cycle inhibitor data in Figure 5A, confirmed the influence of cell cycle stages on USP18 induction. The G1/S stages allow rapid induction of expression induction, but the G2 stage restrains the initiation of gene induction, resulting in a prolonged delay in USP18 expression.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cell cycle reporter and synchronization experiments.

claims.claim: The promoter of USP18 contains a large number of CpG sites, which are highly methylated in all cell types examined.
claims.source: Intriguingly, the promoter of USP18 contains a large number of CpG sites, which are highly methylated in all the cell types examined.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of genome-wide DNA methylation profiles.

claims.claim: The IRF9 promoter contains less CpG sites and is less methylated than the USP18 promoter.
claims.source: In contrast, the IRF9 promoter contains less CpG sites and is less methylated (Komaki, 2018; Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of genome-wide DNA methylation profiles and citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Decitabine treatment reduces the fraction of cells with prolonged delay times in USP18 induction.
claims.source: We observed that the decitabine treatment reduced the fraction of cells with prolonged delay times in USP18 induction, which is in part due to earlier USP18 upregulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 4), supporting that the promoter methylation inhibits USP18 induction (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using decitabine treatment shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: Promoter methylation inhibits USP18 induction.
claims.source: We observed that the decitabine treatment reduced the fraction of cells with prolonged delay times in USP18 induction, which is in part due to earlier USP18 upregulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 4), supporting that the promoter methylation inhibits USP18 induction (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that decitabine (a DNA methyltransferase inhibitor) reduces USP18 induction delay.

claims.claim: Cell cycle stages impact the initiation of USP18 upregulation through modulating the promoter methylation level.
claims.source: In summary, our results suggested that the cell cycle stages may impact the initiation of USP18 upregulation through modulating the promoter methylation level.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing the effects of cell cycle stages and DNA methylation on USP18 induction.

claims.claim: The open window length for immediate USP18 induction is estimated to be 7.3 hrs (~33% of 21.82 hrs cell cycle length).
claims.source: The model was fit to the experimentally-determined distribution of USP18 delay times within a cell cycle (Figure 6B; the data from Figure 4E) and we obtained an estimate of the open window length to be 7.3 hrs (~33% of 21.82 hrs).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling fitted to experimental data.

claims.claim: The 24-hr pretreatment effectively induces USP18 upregulation to a much higher extent than 2-hr and 10-hr pretreatments.
claims.source: We observed that the 24-hr pretreatment effectively induced UPS18 upregulation, to a much higher extent than those upon 2-hr and 10-hr pretreatments.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by stochastic simulations of the computational model.

claims.claim: Higher levels of USP18 expression by prolonged pretreatment lead to reduced IRF9 induction upon the second stimulation at the single-cell level.
claims.source: Importantly, as shown in Figure 6C, the higher levels of USP18 expression by the prolonged pretreatment lead to reduced IRF9 induction upon the second stimulation at the single-cell level, qualitatively in agreement with our experimental data (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by both computational modeling and experimental data shown in Figure 6C and 6D.

claims.claim: IFN-α is a member of the type I IFN family of cytokines.
claims.source: IFN-α is a member of the type I IFN family of cytokines, which are synthesized and secreted in mammals upon pathogen infection and initiate innate immune responses to limit pathogen spread via reducing protein production, upregulating antiproliferative and antiviral genes, and programmed cell death (Schneider et al., 2014; Barber and defense, 2001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Type I IFNs are synthesized and secreted in mammals upon pathogen infection and initiate innate immune responses.
claims.source: IFN-α is a member of the type I IFN family of cytokines, which are synthesized and secreted in mammals upon pathogen infection and initiate innate immune responses to limit pathogen spread via reducing protein production, upregulating antiproliferative and antiviral genes, and programmed cell death (Schneider et al., 2014; Barber and defense, 2001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: IFN-α has been clinically used in treatments of hepatitis B and C infection, HIV infection, melanoma, kidney cancer, leukemia and lymphoma.
claims.source: IFN-α has also been clinically used in treatments of a variety of diseases, such as hepatitis B and C infection, HIV infection, melanoma, kidney cancer, leukemia and lymphoma (Watanabe et al., 2013; Medrano et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: IFN-α exerts its anti-pathogenic and anti-proliferative effects by activating the JAK-STAT pathway, leading to the expression of over 300 IFN-stimulated genes (ISGs).
claims.source: IFN-α exerts its anti-pathogenic and anti-proliferative effects by activating the Janus kinase (JAK)-signal transducer and activator of transcription (STAT) pathway, leading to the expression of over 300 IFN-stimulated genes (ISGs) (Schneider et al., 2014; Schoggins and Rice, 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: IFN-α binds to IFNAR, triggering the activation of JAK1 and TYK2, which phosphorylate STAT1 and STAT2.
claims.source: IFN-α binds to a heterodimeric transmembrane receptor, the IFN-α receptor (IFNAR), triggering the activation of receptor-associated kinases Janus kinase 1 (JAK1) and tyrosine kinase 2 (TYK2), which in turn phosphorylate transcription factors signal transducer and activator of transcription 1 (STAT1) and STAT2.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work and represents established knowledge of the IFN-α signaling pathway.

claims.claim: Phosphorylated STAT1 and STAT2 dimerize and associate with IRF9 to form ISGF3 complex.
claims.source: The phosphorylated STAT1 and STAT2 dimerize and associate with IFN-regulatory factor 9 (IRF9) to form IFN-stimulated gene factor 3 (ISGF3) complex.
claims.evidence: This claim represents established knowledge of the IFN-α signaling pathway.

claims.claim: ISGF3 translocates to the nucleus and binds to ISRE, activating the transcription of ISGs.
claims.source: ISGF3 then translocates to the nucleus and binds to the DNA consensus sequences, known as IFN-stimulated response element (ISRE), activating the transcription of ISGs (Platanias, 2005; Schreiber, 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work and represents established knowledge.

claims.claim: A response that is too short or too weak will fail to limit pathogen spread.
claims.source: A response that is too short or too weak will fail to limit pathogen spread, whereas a response that is too prolonged or too strong will result in tissue damage, organ failure, and carcinogenesis (Choubey and Moudgil, 2011; Crow, 2016; McNab et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: A response that is too prolonged or too strong will result in tissue damage, organ failure, and carcinogenesis.
claims.source: A response that is too short or too weak will fail to limit pathogen spread, whereas a response that is too prolonged or too strong will result in tissue damage, organ failure, and carcinogenesis (Choubey and Moudgil, 2011; Crow, 2016; McNab et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: In some studies, prior exposure to IFN-α accelerates cells' responses to the second IFN input, enabling a 'priming' effect.
claims.source: In some studies, a prior exposure to IFN-α accelerates cells' responses to the second IFN input, enabling a 'priming' effect (Abreu et al., 1979; Kuri et al., 2009; Rodriguez-Pla et al., 2014; Phipps-Yonas et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: In other studies, pretreatment with IFN-α diminishes the responses to the following stimulation, resulting in a 'desensitization' effect.
claims.source: In other studies, however, a pretreatment with IFN-α diminishes the responses to the following stimulation, resulting in a 'desensitization' effect (Scagnolari and Antonelli, 2018; Sarasin-Filipowicz et al., 2009; Makowska et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The priming effect can be attributed to the expression induction of IRF9, STAT1 and STAT2, which are components of ISGF3 transcriptional complex.
claims.source: Previous studies have demonstrated that the priming effect can be attributed to the expression induction of IRF9, STAT1 and STAT2, which are components of ISGF3 transcriptional complex that mediates IFN-driven gene expression (Cheon et al., 2013), and IFN-induced chromatin modifications (Kamada et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: IFN-induced chromatin modifications contribute to the priming effect.
claims.source: Previous studies have demonstrated that the priming effect can be attributed to the expression induction of IRF9, STAT1 and STAT2, which are components of ISGF3 transcriptional complex that mediates IFN-driven gene expression (Cheon et al., 2013), and IFN-induced chromatin modifications (Kamada et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: USP18 is a major negative regulator of JAK-STAT signaling.
claims.source: To determine the mechanism of desensitization caused by the prolonged pretreatment, we use a short hairpin RNA (shRNA) to knock-down the expression of ubiquitin-specific peptidase 18 (USP18), a major negative regulator of JAK-STAT signaling that we identified previously (Zou et al., 2007; Kim et al., 2008; Ritchie et al., 2004; Malakhova et al., 2003), in the reporter cell line (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, USP18-KD).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: USP18 is transcriptionally upregulated by IFN treatment and exerts inhibition of IFN-α signaling at the receptor level, forming a negative feedback loop.
claims.source: USP18 is transcriptionally upregulated by IFN treatment and exerts inhibition of IFN-α signaling at the receptor level, forming a negative feedback loop (Sarasin-Filipowicz et al., 2009; François-Newton et al., 2011; Arimoto et al., 2017; Malakhova et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Individual cells respond to IFNs in a highly heterogeneous manner, both in vitro and in vivo.
claims.source: Recent studies found that individual cells respond to IFNs in a highly heterogeneous manner, both in vitro (Czerkies et al., 2018; Rand et al., 2012; Patil et al., 2015) and in vivo (Miao et al., 2010; Stifter et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Traditional assays that measure averaged responses across populations at static time points may not accurately characterize cells' responses to IFNs.
claims.source: Therefore, traditional assays that measure averaged responses across populations at static time points may not be able to accurately characterize cells' responses to IFNs.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of heterogeneous single-cell responses.

claims.claim: A rapid nuclear translocation of STAT1 (within ~0.5 hr) is observed in response to IFN-α stimulation.
claims.source: We observed a rapid nuclear translocation (within ~0.5 hr) of STAT1 followed by a gradual increase in PIRF9-driven gene expression in response to IFN-α stimulation (Figure 1B and C; Video 1), consistent with traditional western blotting results (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claims.claim: STAT1 nuclear translocation correlates temporally with the increase in PIRF9-driven transcriptional activity.
claims.source: STAT1 nuclear translocation correlated temporally with the increase in PIRF9-driven transcriptional activity (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: A dose higher than 10 ng/ml IFN-α is required for desensitization in 24-hr pretreatment.
claims.source: We also examined how changing the dose of IFN pretreatment impacts the effect on the response to the second input and found that a dose higher than 10 ng/ml is required for desensitization in 24-hr pretreatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 3, A–C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3, A–C.

claims.claim: The effect of desensitization decreases as a function of break time between pretreatment and second stimulation.
claims.source: Furthermore, we tested how the break time between pretreatment and second stimulation influences desensitization and found that the effect of desensitization decreased as a function of break time (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: IRF9 is one of the major early response ISGs and encodes a key component of the ISGF3 complex.
claims.source: We chose IRF9 because it has been well defined as one of the major early response ISGs and it encodes a key component of the ISGF3 complex (Cheon et al., 2013; Tsuno et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: 100 ng/ml (10,000 IU/ml) IFN-α is a sub-saturating and clinically relevant concentration.
claims.source: We examined single-cell responses to various doses of IFN-α (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and chose 100 ng/ml (10,000 IU/ml), a sub-saturating and clinically relevant (Tarhini et al., 2012) concentration, for the following analyses.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work and experimental dose-response data.

claims.claim: The heterogeneity in upstream components (STAT1 and IRF9) contributes partially to cell-to-cell variation in the expression levels of USP18.
claims.source: To determine the source of clonal heterogeneity in USP18 induction, we analyzed the relationship of USP18 expression with STAT1 or IRF9 expression at the single-cell level and found that the heterogeneity in these upstream components contributed partially to cell-to-cell variation in the expression levels of USP18.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data analyzing correlations between USP18 and upstream components.

claims.claim: The delay times of USP18 upregulation correlate poorly with STAT1 or IRF9 expression.
claims.source: However, the delay times of USP18 upregulation correlated poorly with STAT1 or IRF9 expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Cell cycle progression is a major factor that coordinates gene expression.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Roscovitine arrests cells in G1 or G1/S stage.

claims.claim: DNA methylation decreases in G1 and increases during S and G2 phases.
claims.source: Previous studies revealed global variations of epigenetic modifications during cell cycle. For instance, DNA methylation decreases in G1 and increases during S and G2 phases (Brown et al., 2007; Woodcock et al., 1986; Desjobert et al., 2015).

claims.claim: Decreased promoter methylation leads to increased USP18 expression in breast cancer.

claims.claim: Decitabine leads to cell cycle arrest in G1 or G2.
claims.source: We note that decitabine also leads to cell cycle arrest in G1 or G2 (Shin et al., 2013; Lavelle et al., 2003).

claims.claim: The accelerating effect of decitabine on USP18 expression is via inhibition of methylation rather than cell cycle arrest.
claims.source: Because only a small fraction of decitabine-treated cells is arrested in G1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 5) and USP18 induction is largely delayed in G2 (Figure 5C), the accelerating effect of decitabine on USP18 expression should be via inhibition of methylation rather than cell cycle arrest.

claims.source: When the duration of pretreatment is shorter than or close to the delay time (e.g. 2- or 10-hr pretreatment), USP18 can only be partially induced in some cells so that the fast-acting positive feedback loop and the priming effect dominate.

claims.claim: The 24-hr pretreatment can fully induce USP18-mediated negative feedback in most cells regardless of their cell cycle stages at treatment onset, resulting in desensitization to subsequent stimulation.

claims.claim: Key regulatory processes can be compartmentalized temporally by the cell cycle to decode dynamically varying signals.

claims.evidence: This claim is a general conclusion inferred from the study's findings.

claims.claim: Regulatory circuits with coupled negative and positive feedback loops can give rise to various dynamic behaviors, such as sustained oscillations and excitable gene expression.
claims.source: Regulatory circuits with coupled negative and positive feedback loops have been discovered in many biological processes, and, depending on the specific mechanisms and kinetics, can give rise to various dynamic behaviors, such as sustained oscillations (Danino et al., 2010; Jiang et al., 2017) and excitable gene expression (Ori et al., 2018; Süel et al., 2006; Mönke et al., 2017).

claims.claim: The coupled feedback system in the JAK-STAT pathway serves as a timer that measures the initial input duration and coordinates the temporal order of regulatory processes with opposing effects.

claims.claim: Delays in the expression of key regulatory factors have been found important for ensuring proper execution of biological functions.

claims.claim: Gene regulatory networks with specific topologies can give rise to delayed gene expression, enabling filtering of transient inputs.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The cell cycle gating revealed in this study represents a new mechanism that leads to delayed induction of specific genes upon stimulation.

results.result: IFN-α pretreatments of different durations lead to opposite effects on transcriptional responses to a second IFN-α input: short pretreatments (2-hr or 10-hr) enhance responses (priming), while prolonged pretreatment (24-hr) dramatically decreases responses (desensitization).
results.evaluation: Claims C5 and C6 provide direct experimental evidence from Figure 1E-F showing enhanced PIRF9-YFP reporter induction with 2-hr and 10-hr pretreatments versus dramatic decrease with 24-hr pretreatment. Claim C1 accurately summarizes these duration-dependent opposite effects. The data are internally consistent and statistically significant (p<0.001).

results.result: USP18 is required for desensitization induced by prolonged IFN-α pretreatment, acting through a delayed negative feedback loop, while a fast-acting positive feedback loop mediates priming effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C10 provide strong experimental evidence that USP18 knockdown abolishes desensitization effects while preserving priming effects across all pretreatment durations. Claim C11 shows specificity by demonstrating SOCS1 knockdown does not affect desensitization. The regulatory network architecture (C2) is supported by both experimental data and computational modeling.

results.result: USP18 upregulation can only be initiated during G1/early S phases of the cell cycle, with cells treated during later phases showing extended delays until the next G1 phase, resulting in heterogeneous single-cell induction kinetics.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C25 provide direct experimental evidence from cell cycle tracking (Figure 4E) showing modest delays when treatment occurs at 0-35% of cell cycle versus extended delays proportional to time until next cycle. Claims C27-C28 provide independent validation using cell cycle synchronization and CDK2/FUCCI reporters (Figure 5A, 5C). The cell-to-cell variability explanation (C26) is well-supported by the data.

results.result: Cell cycle gating provides temporal compartmentalization of feedback loops, enabling duration-dependent desensitization: short pretreatments allow only partial USP18 induction with priming dominating, while 24-hr pretreatment (longer than full cell cycle) induces USP18 in most cells regardless of cell cycle stage, causing desensitization.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C74 provide mechanistic interpretation supported by experimental data showing cell cycle-dependent USP18 induction and computational modeling. The temporal compartmentalization concept (C4, C75) logically integrates the cell cycle gating mechanism with the observed duration-dependent effects. The 24-hr pretreatment exceeding the 21.82-hr cell cycle length (C72) provides quantitative support.

results.result: IRF9 and USP18 exhibit strikingly different activation kinetics despite being induced by the same JAK-STAT signaling: IRF9 shows fast, uniform induction (mean 7.9±0.2 hrs) while USP18 shows slow, heterogeneous induction (mean 12.2±0.2 hrs) with 16.7% of cells exhibiting prolonged delays >10 hrs.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C23 provide quantitative experimental data from the dual reporter cell line (Figure 4C) with precise measurements of activation times and statistical parameters. The bimodal distribution of USP18 delay times (C22) is directly observed. The striking difference in kinetics (C19) is well-documented with confidence intervals provided.

results.result: Computational modeling suggests an ~8-hour delay in USP18 upregulation is required to reproduce experimental observations, and predicts that repetitive short pulses should produce higher transcriptional responses than sustained input, which was experimentally validated.
results.evaluation: Claim C15 shows systematic model fitting identified 8-hr delay as optimal (Figure 3B-C). The model prediction (C16) was experimentally tested and confirmed (C17): 5×8-hr pulses produced higher response than 40-hr sustained input. Claim C18 demonstrates this difference is USP18-dependent, validating the model mechanism. The integration of modeling and experimental validation is rigorous.

results.result: The USP18 promoter contains highly methylated CpG sites, and DNA methylation inhibits USP18 induction, with cell cycle stages potentially impacting USP18 upregulation through modulating promoter methylation levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C31 are supported by genome-wide methylation data. Claim C32 shows decitabine reduces USP18 delay times, supporting C33. However, C34 is speculative as the direct link between cell cycle stages and promoter methylation changes at the USP18 locus is not demonstrated. The mechanism remains incompletely characterized despite suggestive evidence.

results.result: Computational modeling incorporating cell cycle gating estimates the open window for immediate USP18 induction at 7.3 hrs (~33% of cell cycle), and stochastic simulations show 24-hr pretreatment induces higher USP18 levels leading to reduced IRF9 induction, qualitatively matching experimental data.
results.evaluation: Claim C35 provides quantitative estimate from model fitting to experimental delay time distribution (Figure 6B). Claims C36-C37 show stochastic simulations qualitatively reproduce single-cell experimental patterns (Figure 6C-D). The authors acknowledge quantitative limitations but demonstrate the model captures key features. The integration of cell cycle gating into the model is well-justified.

results.result: USP18-mediated desensitization attenuates the antiviral effect of prolonged IFN-α pretreatment, with USP18 knockdown showing ~15-fold greater viral suppression than wild-type cells.
results.evaluation: Claim C12 provides quantitative viral replication data (Figure 2—figure supplement 4) showing dramatic difference between WT and USP18-KD. Claim C13 correctly interprets this as USP18-mediated desensitization attenuating antiviral effects. The functional consequence of the molecular mechanism is clearly demonstrated.

results.result: STAT1 shows rapid nuclear translocation within ~0.5 hr in response to IFN-α stimulation, correlating temporally with increased PIRF9-driven transcriptional activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C56 are supported by time-lapse imaging data (Figure 1B-C) and validated by western blotting (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D). The temporal correlation between STAT1 translocation and transcriptional activity is clearly demonstrated. This establishes the basic response dynamics of the system.

results.result: Desensitization in 24-hr pretreatment requires IFN-α doses >10 ng/ml, and the desensitization effect decreases as a function of break time between pretreatment and second stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C58 are supported by dose-response experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) and break time experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 4). These characterize important parameters of the desensitization phenomenon, though they are secondary to the main findings about duration-dependence and mechanism.

results.result: Heterogeneity in upstream components (STAT1 and IRF9) contributes partially to cell-to-cell variation in USP18 expression levels, but delay times of USP18 upregulation correlate poorly with STAT1 or IRF9 expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C62 are supported by single-cell correlation analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 2). This negative result is important as it rules out upstream heterogeneity as the primary source of USP18 delay variability, motivating the investigation of cell cycle effects. The analysis is appropriate for identifying sources of heterogeneity.

results.result: The length of a full cell cycle in the reporter cell line was estimated to be 21.82 hrs based on single-cell time trace measurements.
results.evaluation: Claim C72 is supported by direct measurement from time-lapse imaging tracking cell divisions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). This parameter is essential for interpreting the relationship between pretreatment duration and cell cycle length, and for computational modeling.

results.result: Reporter cell lines were constructed using CRISPR/Cas9 to tag STAT1 with mCherry, insert YFP under the IRF9 promoter with P2A spacer, and insert CFP with NLS under the USP18 promoter with P2A spacer.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C93 describe the construction of reporter cell lines validated by PCR, sequencing, FACS, and western blotting (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1). The methodological approach is well-documented and the reporters function as intended based on the data presented.

results.result: Background information on IFN-α signaling, JAK-STAT pathway components, clinical applications, and prior literature on priming and desensitization effects.
results.evaluation: These claims (C38-C52, C59, C63-C69) represent established knowledge from the literature, properly cited. They provide necessary context for the study but do not constitute novel findings. The citations appear appropriate and the background information is accurately presented.

results.result: Individual cells respond to IFNs heterogeneously, traditional population-based assays may not accurately characterize responses, and 100 ng/ml IFN-α is a sub-saturating, clinically relevant concentration.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C54 cite prior literature on single-cell heterogeneity, motivating the single-cell approach. Claim C60 is supported by dose-response data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and citation. These provide methodological justification but are not primary findings.

results.result: The coupled feedback system in the JAK-STAT pathway serves as a timer measuring input duration, representing a new mechanism for delayed gene induction distinct from other known mechanisms like nucleosome occupancy or network topology.
results.evaluation: Claims C76, C78-C80 cite prior work on feedback loops and delay mechanisms. Claims C77 and C81 present the novel conceptual contribution: cell cycle gating as a timer and new delay mechanism. This interpretation is well-supported by the experimental and modeling data, though it represents a conceptual advance rather than a discrete experimental finding.

results.result: Speculative implications include: external conditions affecting cell cycle could modulate IFN responsiveness, cancer stem cell resistance may relate to G0/G1 residence time, G2/M inhibitors may enhance IFN effects, SARS-CoV-2 sensitivity to IFNs suggests therapeutic strategies, and repetitive short IFN administrations or USP18 inhibitors may enhance effectiveness.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C84, C88-C90 are explicitly speculative or cite single studies without direct experimental validation in this work. While these are reasonable hypotheses based on the findings, they represent future directions rather than established results. C88 cites recent literature but C89-C90 are untested predictions.

results.result: Other mechanisms contribute to priming (histone H3 methylation) and desensitization (SOCS proteins), and 114 of 278 ISGs examined have >100 CpG sites in their promoters besides USP18.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C86 cite prior literature acknowledging other regulatory mechanisms. Claim C87 presents descriptive data from genome-wide analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A). These provide context but are not central findings of the study.

results.result: The coefficients of variation for IRF9 and USP18 activation times are 0.5558 and 0.4429 respectively, and 16.48% of cells show delays >10 hrs (Group 2).
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C95 provide statistical parameters from experimental data (Figure 4C-D). These quantitative descriptors characterize the heterogeneity observed but are secondary metrics rather than primary findings.
